Marie Curie was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw on 7 November 1867. Poland was then part of the Russian Empire [1]. She moved to Paris to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne, where she met the physicist Pierre Curie and married him [2]. In 1898 the couple discovered two new radioactive elements in pitchblende ore: polonium, named after Poland, and radium [1].

In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Henri Becquerel, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own. She is still the only person to win Nobels in two different sciences [1]. Pierre died in 1906, and that same year she took over his teaching post, becoming the first woman professor at the University of Paris [1]. Radium institutes were later set up for her in Paris and Warsaw. During World War I she set up portable X-ray units to help treat wounded French soldiers [2].

Her elder daughter, Irène Joliot-Curie, also won a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, together with her husband Frédéric Joliot [2]. Marie Curie died on 4 July 1934 from illness caused by years of handling radioactive material. Sources disagree on the exact diagnosis: some say aplastic anemia, others leukemia [1][2]. In 1995 she became the first woman buried in the Panthéon in Paris for her own achievements [1].
